title: Common Pitfalls
html:
Most ML failures are process bugs, not algorithm choices. This checklist collects the classic ones with their symptoms and fixes.

PitfallSymptomFix
Data leakageOffline scores too good; collapse in productionSplit first, Pipeline, check feature availability at prediction time (see Data Leakage)
Duplicates / same entity across splitsNear-perfect validation scoresDeduplicate; group splits
Random split of time-ordered dataProduction worse than validationTime-based split / TimeSeriesSplit
Accuracy on imbalanced dataHigh accuracy, useless modelPR-AUC, recall/precision, cost; baseline comparison
No baselineCan't tell if the model adds valueDummy model + existing rule
Tuning on the test setTest score optimistic; disappointment laterValidation/CV for all choices; nested CV
Overfitting the validation setMany experiments, tiny “wins” that don't replicateLarger validation set, repeated CV, report variance
Preprocessing fitted on all dataSlightly-to-very optimistic scoresFit scalers/encoders/imputers/selectors inside CV
Training–serving skewSame input, different prediction online vs offlineOne shared feature pipeline; log production features and compare
Distribution shiftSlow decay after launchMonitor inputs/outputs, retrain (see Deployment, Monitoring & MLOps)
Spurious correlations (shortcut learning)Great on validation, fails on new sourcesError analysis, explainability, test on data from other sources/times
Selection / sampling biasModel fails on groups under-represented in trainingFix collection; slice metrics
Label noisePlateaued accuracy; confident “errors” that are rightAudit labels, agreement metrics, clean the test set
Unscaled features for distance/regularised modelsk-NN/SVM/Lasso behave oddlyScale inside the pipeline
Single run, no uncertaintyImprovements within noiseCV mean ± std, confidence intervals, significance tests
Deep learning on small tabular dataHours of tuning, worse than a forestStart with linear models and gradient boosting

Demo: duplicates across the split

Random labels — nothing to learn — but each row appears three times. A random split puts copies of test rows into training, and a 1-nearest-neighbour model “recognises” them:

Before you trust a result

  1. Is there a baseline, and does the model clearly beat it?
  2. Was the split done first, and by time/group where needed?
  3. Is every feature available at prediction time?
  4. Is all preprocessing inside the pipeline?
  5. Is the metric the one the business cares about, at the threshold that will be used?
  6. Is the improvement larger than the run-to-run variance?
  7. Has the test set been used only once?
What are the most common mistakes in ML projects?

Leakage (target leakage, preprocessing before splitting, duplicates or groups across splits, random splits of time series), evaluating with the wrong metric (accuracy on imbalanced data), no baseline, tuning on the test set, and ignoring training–serving skew and drift after deployment.

A model does great offline but poorly in production. What could be wrong?

Leakage in offline evaluation, training–serving skew (features computed differently online), distribution or concept drift since the training data, a different population in production (selection bias), or a threshold chosen for a different base rate. Compare logged production features and predictions with the training data to find out which.
